units.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
units.summary: Which nouns take a/an and plurals — and which never do.

cards.title: Two kinds of noun
cards.body:
**Countable** nouns have singular and plural forms and can take *a/an*: a job, two jobs.
**Uncountable** nouns have no plural and no *a/an*: information, advice, research, equipment, knowledge, evidence, traffic, furniture, homework, money, pollution, progress, transport, accommodation.
examples: There is a lot of evidence that exercise improves health.
She gave me some useful advice.

cards.title: Counting uncountables
cards.body: Use a unit: **a piece of** advice/information/equipment, **an item of** news, **a lot of / much / little** + uncountable.
examples: One piece of research found that…
There isn't much traffic at night.

cards.title: Which words go with which
rows: many, few, a few, a number of, several, each
much, little, a little, an amount of
some, any, a lot of, lots of, more, most, no

items: She gave me some advice / a piece of advice.
A large amount of people use buses.
A large number of people use buses.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Examiners notice 'researches', 'evidences', 'advices'. Fixing them is one of the quickest ways to raise your Grammar band.
examples: Recent research suggests that cities need more green spaces.
Public transport reduces the amount of traffic in city centres.

practice.q: There were too ___ cars on the road.
There is too ___ traffic in Dhaka.
Many [researches] show that sleep affects memory.
A large [amount] of students failed the test.
Let me give you a piece of ___ (advice).

o: There are many evidences for this.
There is much evidence for this.
There is many evidence for this.
practice.a: There is much evidence for this.
There is a lot of evidence for this theory.

units.title: a, an and the
units.summary: First mention, specific things, and things that are unique.

cards.title: a / an
cards.body: Use **a/an** with a singular countable noun when it is **one of many** or **mentioned for the first time**. Use **an** before a vowel **sound**: an hour, an MBA, but a university, a European.
examples: She works as an engineer.
I read an interesting article yesterday.

cards.title: the
cards.body: Use **the** when the reader knows **which one**: it was mentioned before, it is unique, or it is made specific by the rest of the phrase.
examples: The article was about climate change.
the sun, the internet, the government, the environment
the population of Japan, the number of tourists

cards.title: Superlatives and ordinals
cards.body: Always **the** with superlatives and first/second/last.
examples: the highest figure, the most popular option, the first year

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Task 1 reports are full of phrases that need **the**: *the number of, the proportion of, the highest, the period, the rest*.
examples: The proportion of students who walked to school fell over the period.

practice.q: He studies at ___ university in Sylhet.
I saw a film last night. [A] film was about space.

o: The internet has changed our lives.
An internet has changed our lives.
practice.a: The internet has changed our lives.
The proportion of older people increased over the period.

units.title: No article: general meaning
units.summary: When to use no article at all, and the with groups and places.

cards.title: General statements
cards.body: Use **no article** with plural and uncountable nouns used in a **general** sense.
examples: Children need exercise.
Technology changes quickly.
Crime is a problem in many cities.

cards.title: General vs specific
cards.body: Add **the** when the meaning becomes specific.
examples: Education is important. (in general)
The education I received was excellent. (specific)

cards.title: the with groups and places
cards.body: **the** + adjective for groups: the elderly, the poor, the young. Countries with plural or 'Republic/Kingdom': the UK, the USA, the Netherlands. No article: most countries, cities, continents: Bangladesh, Asia.
examples: The elderly often feel isolated.
She moved from Bangladesh to the UK.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Task 2 statements are usually general. Over-using **the** is one of the most common errors in band 5–6 essays.
examples: Governments should invest in education and healthcare.
Young people today face more pressure than previous generations.

practice.q: ___ crime has fallen in many cities.
___ crime that was reported last year was mostly theft.
The governments should invest more in [the] education.

practice.a: Children should learn about money at school.

units.title: Quantifiers: some, any, much, many, few, little

cards.title: some and any
cards.body: **some** in positive sentences and offers; **any** in negatives and questions.
examples: There are some good universities here.
Are there any questions?

cards.title: few / a few, little / a little
cards.body: **a few / a little** = some (positive). **few / little** = not many / not much (negative).
examples: A few students passed. (some did)
Few students passed. (almost none did)
I have a little time. / I have little time.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: 'Few' and 'little' express criticism or a small amount precisely in Task 2 and Part 3.
examples: Few people can afford houses in the capital.
Little attention has been paid to this problem.

practice.q: I have ___ friends in Dhaka, so I'm not lonely.
There is ___ hope of finding survivors now.
There are [a little] parks in the city centre.

practice.a: Few people walk to work in this city.

units.title: all, most, none, each, both, either, neither
units.summary: Comparing groups and proportions — essential for Task 1.

cards.title: most / most of the
cards.body: **most + noun** for things in general; **most of the + noun** for a specific group.
examples: Most people own a phone.
Most of the students in my class live nearby.

cards.title: Proportion language
cards.body: **all, the majority of, more than half of, around a third of, a minority of, very few, none of**
examples: The majority of respondents preferred online shopping.
None of the countries reached 50%.

cards.title: each, every, both, either, neither
cards.body: **each / every + singular noun** and singular verb. **both** = the two together. **either** = one or the other. **neither** = not one and not the other.
examples: Each country has its own system.
Both cities grew, but neither reached a million.

items: Neither of the options are good.
Neither of the options is good.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Pie charts and surveys need proportion language instead of only percentages.
examples: Just over half of the energy came from coal, while renewables accounted for only a tenth.

practice.q: ___ students in my class passed the exam.
Both cities grew, but ___ of them doubled in size.
practice.x: Not one and not the other.

practice.q: Every [students] must bring an ID card.
Just over ___ (half) of the respondents chose option A.

o: The majority of people prefers cars.
The majority of people prefer cars.
practice.a: The majority of people prefer cars.
practice.x: 'The majority of' + plural noun usually takes a plural verb.

practice.a: Around a third of the energy came from gas.

units.title: Pronouns and reference: it, this, they, such

cards.title: Pointing back
cards.body: Use **it / they / this / these / that / such + noun** to refer to ideas already mentioned. This creates cohesion without repetition.
examples: Many governments have introduced sugar taxes. This policy has reduced consumption.
Some people prefer to rent. They argue that it gives them freedom.

cards.title: this + noun is clearest
cards.body: A bare **this** can be unclear. Add a summary noun: *this problem, this trend, this approach, such measures*.
examples: Traffic is increasing. This trend is likely to continue.

items: The government should help students. It should give it money.
The government should give students financial support.
Pollution is a problem. They cause disease.
Pollution is a problem. It causes disease.
Pronoun must agree with its noun.
Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Band 7 Coherence and Cohesion needs **clear referencing**. Replacing 'Moreover' with 'This…' often improves flow.
examples: Fast food is cheap and convenient. As a result of this, many families rely on it.

practice.q: Cities are becoming crowded. ___ makes housing expensive.
Many students work part-time. ___ often struggle to find time to study.
Social media is popular, but [they] can be addictive.
Many people [they] believe that money brings happiness.

o: Prices rose. This made it hard.
Prices rose sharply. This increase made housing unaffordable for many.
practice.a: Prices rose sharply. This increase made housing unaffordable for many.
Such measures could reduce traffic significantly.

units.title: Possessives and compound nouns
units.summary: The children's books, the city's population, a car park.

cards.title: 's and of
cards.body: Use **'s** with people, animals, countries and organisations; **of** with things and longer phrases.
examples: the country's economy
my parents' house
the population of the city
the end of the year

cards.title: Compound nouns
cards.body: Two nouns together; the first works like an adjective and is usually singular.
examples: a car park, a bus station, a ten-year plan, a three-day course

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Map and Task 1 descriptions use many compound nouns.
examples: The car park was replaced by a shopping centre.

practice.q: My ___ (parents) house is near the river.

practice.a: A new bus station was built near the market.

units.title: Nominalisation: academic noun phrases
units.summary: Turning verbs and adjectives into nouns for a concise, formal style.

cards.title: From verb to noun
cards.body: Academic writing often uses **nouns** where speech uses verbs. It sounds more objective and lets you pack ideas into the subject.
examples: Prices increased → The increase in prices…
People consume more meat → Higher meat consumption…
The government failed to act → The government's failure to act…

cards.title: Common pairs
rows: an increase in, a decrease in

items: The increase of prices was sharp.
The increase in prices was sharp.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Nominalisation is a hallmark of band 7+ writing: flexible, precise and less personal.
examples: The rapid growth of cities has put pressure on public services.
A reduction in car use would improve air quality.

practice.q: The ___ (develop) of new technology has changed work.

o: Because people use cars more, the air is dirty.
Increased car use has led to a decline in air quality.
practice.a: Increased car use has led to a decline in air quality.

practice.q: Rewrite with a noun subject: 'Cities grew rapidly, so housing became expensive.'
practice.a: The rapid growth of cities made housing expensive.
